title: Examples and Output Contracts
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to distinguish an illustrative example from an output contract and to check generated JSON in two stages: parsing its syntax and validating its application-specific requirements.
objectives: Distinguish an example output from a contract that defines required output characteristics.
Determine whether text can be parsed as JSON before checking its application-specific structure.
Identify outputs that are valid JSON but do not satisfy a stated output contract.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with objects, arrays, strings, and data fields, but it does not assume experience with a particular model provider or product.

For this module, an example is one illustration of acceptable output. An output contract is the set of application-specific requirements against which an output will be checked. This local definition can include the required top-level value, field names, and field value types.

sections.title: Separate the illustration from the requirements
paragraphs: Consider the example output {"status":"ready","items":[]}. It illustrates one object containing a status string and an items array. By itself, the example does not state whether other fields are permitted, whether status may have other string values, or whether items may contain values.

A corresponding contract must state the requirements explicitly. For this exercise, the contract is: the complete output must be exactly one JSON object; the object must contain a status field whose value is a string and an items field whose value is an array; and no commentary may appear outside the object. These are application-specific requirements defined by this module, not requirements imposed on every JSON object.

sections.title: Parse first, then validate the contract
paragraphs: JSON is a text format for serialized structured data. A JSON object begins with {, ends with }, and contains name-value members. JSON strings use quotation marks and defined escape sequences, and literal control characters are not permitted inside strings.

JSON.parse converts conforming JSON text into the corresponding ECMAScript value. If parsing fails, it throws a SyntaxError. JSON whitespace may surround the serialized value, but prose or other commentary outside that value does not belong to the JSON text accepted by the parsing grammar.

Successful parsing establishes that the text follows JSON syntax. It does not establish the application-specific contract defined in the previous section. After parsing, check that the top-level value is an object, that status is present and is a string, and that items is present and is an array.

For example, {"status":3,"items":[]} is valid JSON, so it can pass the parsing stage. It fails this module's contract because the status value is a number rather than a string. The text Result: {"status":"ready","items":[]} fails the parsing stage because Result: is commentary outside the serialized object.

questions.prompt: What does the example {"status":"ready","items":[]} establish by itself?
choices: It illustrates one possible output but does not define every permitted value or field.
It proves that status must always equal ready in every application.
It permits commentary before and after the object.
questions.explanation: The module distinguishes an illustration from explicit requirements. The example shows one possible object, while the contract must separately state required fields, types, and boundaries.

questions.prompt: Under the contract in this module, which output passes JSON parsing but fails the application-specific field requirements?
questions.explanation: The first choice is valid JSON, but status is a number instead of the string required by the contract. The second satisfies both stages. The third contains commentary outside the JSON object and therefore fails parsing.

questions.prompt: Why should an application check the contract after JSON parsing succeeds?
choices: Parsing checks JSON syntax, while the later check enforces required fields and value types.
Parsing already guarantees every application-specific requirement.
The later check converts commentary into valid JSON.
questions.explanation: The module explains that parsing establishes syntactic validity. Requirements such as a string-valued status field and an array-valued items field must be checked separately.
